title: Love and mercy between you
hookLine: He made mates for you to find rest in, and put love and mercy between you (30:21)

cards: At many Muslim weddings, at some point, someone reads one particular verse. You'll often find it on the invitation too, in Arabic calligraphy, sometimes in gold.

Plenty of people know it without knowing much else of Surah Ar-Rum. It's short, and it sits in a list of God's signs, between the creation of human beings from dust and the creation of the heavens and earth.
It puts a marriage, an ordinary household, right there among them.

teach.b: Pickthall: "And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." In that, the verse ends, are signs for people who reflect.
From yourselves: of the same kind, the same nature. Then the purpose: li-taskunu ilayha, that you might find rest in them.
The root s-k-n means stillness, settling, dwelling; it gives sakina, tranquility, and maskan, a home.

teach.h: SAKAN: A PLACE TO COME TO REST.
teach.b: So a spouse is somewhere you come to rest, the way you come home. Then two words, carefully chosen. Mawadda: warm affection, love you can see.
And rahma: mercy, from the same root as the womb, and as ar-Rahman. Commentators have enjoyed setting the two side by side.

Some say mawadda is the love of the early years, and rahma what carries a couple when looks fade and someone gets ill. Others say mawadda is love you feel, and rahma is care you choose, even on days the feeling is thin.
Either way, the verse doesn't stop at love; it adds mercy, as if love alone won't always be enough.
And God put them there, ja'ala baynakum: not you made them, He placed them between you. Many Muslims hear that as a reason for gratitude, and as a standard.
A hadith in Tirmidhi says the best of you are those who are best to their families. The Qur'an counts a quiet kitchen, two people at rest with each other, as a sign as real as the sky.

how: 30:21 is widely recited at Muslim weddings and written on wedding cards and gifts, and Muslims often describe marriage through its words: rest, love and mercy.

o: warm, visible love, placed between two people
a formal greeting exchanged between families
a marriage contract signed before witnesses

games.q: love and mercy — tap the pairs.
p: the root of sakina and maskan
mercy, from the root of the womb

s: the verse sits in a list of God's signs
between the creation of humans and of the heavens and earth.
it pairs love, mawadda, with mercy, rahma.
the verse says spouses create love and mercy themselves
it says God placed them between you, ja'ala baynakum.

games.q: years into a marriage, the warm feeling is thin today. according to the commentators, what does the verse's second word offer?
o: mercy: care you choose, even when feeling is thin.
games.why: many commentators say rahma carries a couple when mawadda fades: the verse pairs love with mercy on purpose.

practice: Think of the person you come home to, or would most like to: a spouse, a parent, a sibling, a friend, a child, and picture their face at the end of an ordinary day.
Ask where your love for them is easy right now, and where it needs mercy instead. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Mawadda. Warm, visible love, one of the two things, with rahma, mercy, that Ar-Rum says God placed between spouses, so they could find rest in one another. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: love and mercy, the two things placed between spouses in 30:21.

carryVoice: Your line: love and mercy between. Rest in each other, with love and mercy placed between. Rest well tonight.

sources.q: And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy.
